questions.q: According to Samsung's US marketing chief, what was Samsung's smartphone problem in 2011?
options: Its phones were technically weaker than the iPhone and reviewers said so
Its phones were priced far above the iPhone, so few people tried them
People knew Samsung for televisions but did not recognise it in smartphones
It had no retail distribution for phones anywhere in the United States
questions.why: It was a branding problem: no recognition of what the phones were or stood for.

questions.q: Advertising that openly mocks the market leader, like Samsung's "Next Big Thing", is most typical of:
options: A market leader defending its share
A challenger trying to grab attention
A brand in the decline stage clearing stock
A monopoly with no rivals
questions.why: Challengers borrow the leader's fame; leaders rarely give rivals free publicity.

questions.q: A firm starts from the factory, focuses on existing products, relies on selling and promotion, and aims for profit through volume. It follows the:
options: Production concept
Marketing concept
Selling concept
Societal marketing concept
questions.why: Factory, existing products, push, volume: the selling arrow in Figure 0.1.

questions.q: Drucker's view of selling and marketing is best captured by:
options: Marketing aims to make selling superfluous, though some selling will always be needed
Good salesmanship makes marketing unnecessary, since a strong sales force can sell anything
Selling and marketing are two names for the same activity, done by the same people
Marketing should replace the sales force entirely, so that no selling is ever needed
questions.why: Know the customer so well that the product sells itself, but some selling remains.

questions.q: Compared with the AMA's 2004 definition, the 2007 definition:
options: Removes customers from the definition
Limits marketing to advertising and promotion
Returns to the flow of goods from producer to consumer
Describes marketing as an activity and names society at large
questions.why: Function became activity; exchanging offerings and society at large were added.

questions.q: In the AMA definition, "delivering" offerings corresponds most closely to which P?
options: Place
Product
Price
Promotion
questions.why: Creating = product, communicating = promotion, delivering = place, exchanging value = price.

questions.q: The earliest official definitions of marketing focused mainly on the flow of goods from producers to consumers. In 4P terms this is chiefly:
options: Product
Place
Price
Promotion
questions.why: Moving goods to where customers are is distribution: Place.

questions.q: When pricing a new smartphone, the class agreed that demand:
options: Should be estimated first from market data, and the price then set to match it
Is irrelevant for a new brand, which has no customers whose demand can be measured
Is fixed by competitors' prices, so the new brand's own price cannot change it
Changes with the price; the task is to find the price threshold customers will accept
questions.why: Price and demand move together; study competitors, the USP and willingness to pay to find the threshold.

questions.q: Mercedes-Benz India's "Retail of the Future" model changed which P most directly?
options: Product
Promotion
Place
Positioning
questions.why: It changed the channel (direct sales with dealers as franchise partners) which in turn affected price.

questions.q: A mother buys a breakfast cereal that her eight-year-old eats. In marketing terms:
options: The mother is the customer and the child the consumer
Both are consumers
The mother is the consumer and the child the customer
Neither is a customer, since the child pays nothing
questions.why: The customer buys; the consumer uses.

questions.q: A distributor who must be offered enough margin to stock your product belongs to which of the 5Cs?
options: Customers
Company
Competitors
Collaborators
questions.why: Collaborators are those who can help you, and must be motivated to.

questions.q: "Should we launch a premium phone while the economy is slowing?" is a question about which C?
options: Company
Context
Competitors
Customers
questions.why: The state of the economy is part of the macro context, the E in PESTLE.

questions.q: The cost of adding a feature, and what customers will pay for it, places "features" in:
options: Company only
Customers only
Both company and customers
Competitors only
questions.why: Cost to provide is a company question; willingness to pay is a customer question.

questions.q: Moving from pricing a smartphone to pricing a breakfast cereal, the class concluded that:
options: The same framework applies, with different emphasis (perishability, seasonality, health trends)
An entirely new framework is needed, because food is bought differently from phones
Only costs matter for a cereal, since buyers of food products compare nothing else
PESTLE does not apply to food products, though the other four Cs still do
questions.why: Frameworks are generic; you change the weights, not the framework.

questions.q: Which of the following is a marketing decision rather than an activity?
options: Conducting an analysis of competitors' prices
Choosing which distributor to appoint in a new state
Tracking the revenue of each region every month
Doing market research among target customers
questions.why: Research, analysis and tracking feed decisions; appointing a distributor is the decision.

questions.q: A participant listed "market selection" under Place. The correct home is:
options: Place, because it concerns geography
Promotion
Product
Targeting, within STP
questions.why: Place means channels; choosing which market to serve is targeting.

questions.q: Packaging decisions belong to which P, as taught in class?
options: Price
Place
Product
Promotion
questions.why: Packaging is part of the product (some argue for a fifth P, but not in this module).

questions.q: STP should generally precede the 4Ps because:
options: The 4Ps are costlier to change than STP, so they are fixed last
STP is strategic and long-term; the 4Ps are tactics that must serve it
The 4Ps are set by finance, and STP by the marketing team
STP is easier to change than price, so it is tried first
questions.why: Segment and position first; then design the mix to deliver them.

questions.q: Changing an established brand's image is called repositioning. The class view was that it is:
options: Very risky, costly and often unsuccessful
Quick and cheap with a new ad campaign
Necessary every year
Only relevant to luxury brands
questions.why: Once an image forms in customers' minds it is hard to move: Maruti's Jimny was the example.

questions.q: Apple sells through few, controlled outlets; Samsung sells almost everywhere. This shows that:
options: Apple's narrow distribution is a mistake that costs it sales
Samsung's wide distribution is a mistake that hurts its image
Each firm's Place follows from its own target and positioning
Distribution is chosen for cost reasons, not for positioning
questions.why: No right or wrong: each mix is aligned to its STP.

questions.q: How can you find out what positioning a company intends for its brand?
options: From how newspapers and television describe the brand
From the company's share price and annual report
From what competitors say about it in their own ads
From its own communication: what its ads say about the brand
questions.why: Intended positioning shows in the company's own communication; actual positioning lives in customers' minds.

questions.q: Tata's own launch ads for the Nano stressed that it was spacious and robust. It still came to be seen as the "cheapest car" mainly because:
options: Tata's own advertising promised the lowest price in the world
Huge media attention to its record-low price fixed that image
Competitors ran comparative ads calling it a poor man's car
Dealers promoted it locally as the cheapest car one could buy
questions.why: The media, not the company, fixed the image, and in India a car is aspirational.

questions.q: Allotting the first Nanos by lottery hurt the brand because:
options: Many cars went to people who already owned bigger cars, who compared it unfavourably
A lottery is not a legal way to sell cars, and the bookings had to be cancelled
The lottery pushed the on-road price well above the promised Rs. 1 lakh
The lottery delayed deliveries by several years, by which time rivals had caught up
questions.why: The intended buyer was a first-time car owner; existing owners spread negative word of mouth.

questions.q: In case analysis, which of the following should you NOT do?
options: State the problem before proposing solutions
List alternatives with pros and cons
Support the recommendation with the case's numbers
Use what the company did after the case date to support your answer
questions.why: Restrict yourself to the information given in the case.

questions.q: Coca-Cola launched Coke Zero alongside Diet Coke mainly to:
options: Offer a completely different health benefit
Replace Diet Coke, which was failing
Reach men, who avoided Diet Coke's feminine image
Lower prices in the cola market
questions.why: Similar benefits, different image: worth the cannibalisation to reach a new segment.

questions.q: According to the professor, the best time for a market leader like Axe to launch a new product or segment is:
options: When sales begin to plateau, or before, while still growing
In the introduction stage, before awareness is built
Only after sales start to decline
Never; leaders should defend their one brand
questions.why: Act from strength, before the challenger arrives at maturity.

questions.q: For an expert business (B2B) buyer, the value that usually matters most is:
options: Psychological value
Economic value
Brand image
Status
questions.why: B2B buyers are knowledgeable; economics comes first, then function.

questions.q: Annual customer revenue Rs. 5,000, 20 loyal years, profit margin 10%, ignoring the discount rate. CLV is:
questions.why: 5,000 × 20 × 10% = 10,000. Forgetting the margin gives the wrong answer of 1,00,000.

questions.q: A friend promises you Rs. 121 two years from now. At a 10% discount rate it is worth today:
options: Rs. 99

questions.q: A firm's retention rate is 80%. The churn rate, and the chance a new customer is still with the firm in year 3, are:
questions.why: Churn = 1 - r = 20%; survival in year 3 = r^(3-1) = 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64.

questions.q: CLV is called the NET present value of future profits because:
options: Taxes are deducted from each year's profit
Only net revenue after returns is counted
Competitors' profits are subtracted
The acquisition cost of the customer is subtracted
questions.why: CLV = discounted future margins minus the acquisition cost.

questions.q: Many dot-com firms collapsed in the early 2000s, in CLV terms, because:
options: Acquisition costs were high and retention so low that margins never covered them
Retention costs were so high that loyal customers became unprofitable
Discount rates were set too low, which made future margins look too large
They captured so much customer data that storage costs outran their margins
questions.why: Customers won with freebies left before paying back the cost of winning them.

questions.q: In standard economic theory, the buyer is assumed to be:
options: Subjective, shaped by culture, and so unpredictable
Guided mainly by emotion, habit and social pressure
Rational only within limits, relying on shortcuts
Rational, utility-maximising and therefore predictable
questions.why: No emotion attached: he weighs every option and maximises utility.

questions.q: Bounded rationality arises because buyers have limited:
options: Cognitive ability, time and information
Income, savings and access to credit
Brand loyalty, trust and experience
Access to shops, stock and delivery
questions.why: These three limits push people to use heuristics.

questions.q: A heuristic leads a buyer to a decision that is:
options: Always optimal
Satisficing: good enough, not necessarily the best
Always irrational
Identical to the economist's prediction
questions.why: Mental shortcuts trade accuracy for speed.

questions.q: Behavioural economics gained momentum after 2002, when the Nobel Prize in economics went to:
options: Richard Thaler
Dan Ariely
Thorstein Veblen
Daniel Kahneman
questions.why: Kahneman, a psychologist, won in 2002; Thaler won in 2017.

questions.q: Two groups estimate the same engineer's salary. One question mentions a low figure, the other a high one, and the second group's estimates are higher. This is:
options: Framing
Availability
Anchoring
Mental accounting
questions.why: A suggested value for an unknown quantity pulls the estimate towards it.

questions.q: Showing "Rs. 4,999" struck through above "Rs. 2,499" mainly uses:
options: Anchoring
Representativeness
The decoy effect
Mental accounting
questions.why: The original price becomes the reference for judging the sale price.

questions.q: An electronics store places its most expensive TVs at the entrance. The intended effect is that shoppers:
options: Buy the most expensive model on display at the entrance
Leave the store quickly because the prices look too high
Compare the price per inch of every screen in the store
Raise the price they consider normal for the TV they came to buy
questions.why: Placement anchors: a Rs. 40-50K budget drifts towards Rs. 70K.

questions.q: Airlines publishing a scheduled time longer than actual flying time, so that flights "arrive early", is an application of:
options: Availability of recent delays
Anchoring on expected time
Scarcity of seats on the flight
The Veblen effect on fares
questions.why: Like Disney's posted wait times, the stated time sets the expectation.

questions.q: "50% of patients survive" produces more yeses than "50% of patients die". This shows:
options: Anchoring
Availability
Framing
Representativeness
questions.why: Same information, presented as a gain versus a loss.

questions.q: A bottle offers "33% more" for the same price. Its effective discount is about:
questions.why: 100 / 1.33 = Rs. 75 a litre, i.e. 25% off.

questions.q: A "25% more" offer is equivalent to a price cut of:
questions.why: 1 / 1.25 = 0.80, so 20% off per unit.

questions.q: Most people choose "33% more" over "33% off" because:
options: "More" is the better deal per litre, as the arithmetic shows
A larger bottle is more convenient to carry home and store
A discount makes buyers doubt the quality of the product
"More" feels like a gain, while a discount is still felt as a loss
questions.why: People prefer gains to reduced losses, even when the reduced loss is worth more.

questions.q: Which statement is a positive frame of the same fact as "8% skipped their second dose"?
options: "Millions are skipping their second dose"
"Vaccines are 92% effective"
"92% returned for their second dose"
"8% of doses are wasted"
questions.why: Same fact presented as a gain: more motivating for people on the fence.

questions.q: The Tata Nano being widely seen as the "cheapest car" is NOT an example of framing because:
options: Framing applies to offers and discounts, not to the image of a product
Framing is how the company presents information; the Nano's image came from media coverage
The Nano was not in fact cheap once taxes and registration were added
Framing works only when a fact is expressed as a percentage or a share
questions.why: The company did not frame it that way: it got positioned by the media.

questions.q: Asked about seven-letter words, people expect more "_ _ _ _ i n g" words than "_ _ _ _ _ n _" words. This is wrong because:
options: Every -ing word also has n in the sixth position, so the n-set is larger
Words ending in -ing are in fact very rare in the pages of a novel
The two sets of words do not overlap, so they cannot be compared
Seven-letter words are too uncommon for either estimate to be right
questions.why: The -ing words are a subset; the error comes from how easily they come to mind.

questions.q: After a bad experience with a brand's smartphone, a buyer avoids its washing machines. This is mainly:
options: Anchoring
The decoy effect
Availability
Mental accounting
questions.why: The easily recalled failure gets high weight, even across unrelated technologies.

questions.q: The class's lesson from MH370 and from AirAsia's 2014 crash was that after a crisis a brand should:
options: Stay silent until all the facts are known
Change its brand name
Cut prices immediately
Communicate early, consistently and with a visible face
questions.why: Silence lets customers create their own narratives; AirAsia's open handling limited the damage.

questions.q: Jingles and taglines matter most in impulse categories because of:
options: Representativeness of the category
Availability at the point of purchase
Mental accounting of small amounts
The Veblen effect on cheap goods
questions.why: What is easily recalled gets picked when buyers do not deliberate.

questions.q: Most people rank "Linda is a bank teller active in a feminist movement" above "Linda is a bank teller". This shows:
options: Representativeness
Anchoring
Framing
Mental accounting
questions.why: Fit to the stereotype beats probability, although (f) is a subset of (d).

questions.q: A new soap uses a translucent bar to signal gentleness, borrowing a cue that Pears made famous. This uses:
options: The decoy effect
Anchoring
Mental accounting
Representativeness
questions.why: The cue fits a pre-existing prototype of a gentle soap.

questions.q: Brand positioning is best described as:
options: A kind of heuristic that customers use to choose quickly
Another name for framing a brand's message as a gain
A strategic choice by the firm, separate from the heuristics customers use
The same as availability, since both are about recall
questions.why: Heuristics describe customer decisions; positioning is part of the firm's STP.

questions.q: X costs $3.00 (quality 5) and Y costs $3.80 (quality 6). Adding Z, priced above X with quality 5, will most likely:
options: Increase the share choosing X
Increase the share choosing Y
Leave choices unchanged
Make most people choose Z
questions.why: Z is dominated by X but not by Y, so fence-sitters move to X.

questions.q: To push buyers towards Y in the same set, a marketer should add an option that is:
options: Clearly inferior to X but not to Y
Clearly inferior to Y but not to X
Better than both X and Y
Identical to X
questions.why: The decoy must be dominated by the option you want to sell.

questions.q: The Economist added a print-only subscription at the same $125 as web-plus-print. Its purpose was to:
options: Sell more print-only subscriptions
Reduce printing costs
Make web-plus-print look like the obvious choice
Test price sensitivity for the web edition
questions.why: Print-only is the decoy; almost nobody chooses it.

questions.q: A shopper always picks the middle-priced option of three, regardless of features. This is called the:
options: Veblen effect
Availability heuristic
Framing effect
Goldilocks effect
questions.why: Not the cheapest, not the dearest: the one in between.

questions.q: Most people would not buy a second concert ticket after losing the first, but would buy one after losing the same amount in cash. This is explained by:
options: Framing
Mental accounting
Anchoring
Representativeness
questions.why: The lost ticket drains the concert account; lost cash drains a general account.

questions.q: Houston airport cut baggage complaints by:
options: Hiring more baggage handlers to unload the aircraft faster
Installing a faster belt that delivered bags in half the time
Offering vouchers to passengers who waited over 8 minutes
Making passengers walk longer so they waited less at the belt
questions.why: Total time stayed the same; occupied walking time is not felt as waiting.

questions.q: An apparel store cut a price from $39 to $34 and sales fell. The most likely reason is that:
options: Prices ending in 9 signal a deal, so $39 looked like an offer
$34 is above a price threshold
Customers expected a higher price for quality
The store ran out of stock
questions.why: 9-endings carry a discount perception; round numbers carry a quality perception.

questions.q: For some luxury goods, demand rises as price rises. This is the:
options: Decoy effect
Framing effect
Veblen (snob) effect
Left-digit effect
questions.why: Exclusivity is the product; a higher price keeps others out: within a range.

questions.q: In the case discussion, the market research had been run in the head-office city rather than in the launch region. The lesson is that:
options: A head-office city is usually a fair sample of the national market
Convenience can bias research; research must represent the market you enter
Market research adds little for consumer goods sold at low prices
Only quantitative research, not interviews, can be relied upon
questions.why: Firms choose what is easy to implement, and the results can mislead.

questions.q: Under A.G. Lafley, P&G's research approach shifted mainly towards:
options: Running larger telephone surveys across more cities each year
Watching consumers in their homes to find nuisances a product could solve
Testing products only in laboratories before any launch
Relying on retailers' sales data to see what customers buy
questions.why: Observation reveals problems people never mention.

questions.q: The session's answer to Steve Jobs's view that customers don't know what they want was that:
options: Research is indeed of little use for products that are truly new, as the iPhone showed
Only a company with Apple's design strength can afford to launch without any research
Customers should be asked to design the products they want, and firms should then build them
Without research the likelihood of failure is higher; the lesson is how research goes wrong
questions.why: Apple's own court documents showed extensive customer research.

questions.q: The Maruti executive who saw a paid respondent at a bus stop illustrates a problem with:
options: The sample: respondents who are not target customers
The wording of questions, which led respondents to an answer
The software used to analyse the data that was collected
The advertising shown to respondents before the interview
questions.why: Feedback from the wrong people misleads.

questions.q: Ethnography differs from ordinary observation research mainly because it:
options: Uses structured questionnaires in place of observation
Takes place in a laboratory under controlled conditions
Is carried out over a longer period, immersed in the community
Uses eye-tracking equipment to record what people notice
questions.why: The researcher lives among users to see how the product fits their lives.

questions.q: Which method is best for revealing how people influence one another's opinions?
options: A mail survey
A focus group
Sales data
An eye-tracking study
questions.why: The New Coke lesson on the slide.

questions.q: Gillette's Vector razor failed in India mainly because it was developed with:
options: Rural Indian men who shaved with a single cup of water
Barbers in Indian cities who shaved many customers a day
Indian students at MIT who shaved with running water
Retailers who wanted a cheaper razor to sell in volume
questions.why: Most Indian men shaved with a cup of water; the blades clogged.

questions.q: The Gillette Guard's success after research in Indian homes shows that:
options: Research must reflect the real conditions of use
Price alone decides which razor succeeds in a poor market
Focus groups held abroad are enough if respondents are Indian
Twin blades are always preferred once buyers have tried them
questions.why: Over 50% volume share within six months of its 2010 launch.

questions.q: New Coke beat old Coke in about 200,000 blind taste tests but failed because the tests missed:
options: How sensitive buyers were to the price of the new drink
Whether bottlers could distribute the new formula in time
How the new can and logo would look on the shelf
The meaning of losing the original and social influence
questions.why: People reacted to what was taken away, and to each other.

questions.q: The slide's lesson from New Coke is that new product development should routinely consider:
options: Social influence effects, which focus groups can reveal
Celebrity endorsement, which taste tests cannot measure
Lower launch prices, which protect a new product
Larger pack sizes, which encourage trial at home
questions.why: Individual tests cannot show social interaction effects.

questions.q: ChotuKool cools its contents to about:
options: Below zero, to make ice
5-15 degrees
20-25 degrees
The same as a regular fridge
questions.why: It is a cooler, not a freezer.

questions.q: Why does ChotuKool open from the top?
options: A top lid looks more modern than a door on the front
A top lid lets the cooler be strapped onto a bicycle
A top lid is cheaper to make than a door with a seal
Cold air sinks, so it stays inside when the lid opens
questions.why: Physics applied to design.

questions.q: The professor's main explanation for ChotuKool's limited success was:
options: Poor distribution in the villages where it was meant to sell
A price that was still too high, and nothing else
Researcher bias: assuming rural buyers want something different from urban buyers
Too little advertising, despite the awards it had won
questions.why: Every stated need was met, but the real aspiration was a proper fridge.

questions.q: Sleepy Owl launched a hot brew because its surveys showed that:
options: People did not want something cold first thing in the morning, even in summer
Cold brew was too expensive for most of its customers
Retailers demanded a product they could sell in winter
Competitors had launched hot brews and were gaining share
questions.why: A format decision driven by customer feedback.

questions.q: Sleepy Owl's recyclable packs came after research showed that:
options: Its packs cost too much to make and squeezed margins
Retailers disliked the shape and wanted smaller packs
A new law required all food packaging to be recyclable
Over 60% of customers felt guilty about its plastic
questions.why: It took a year of research to create them.

questions.q: After Tropicana's pack redesign, its sales fell about 20% in under two months while category sales:
options: Also fell 20%
Did not change
Rose 20%
Fell 50%
questions.why: The loss was Tropicana's alone.

questions.q: The main reason for Tropicana's fall, as discussed in class, was that:
options: The juice formula was changed and regular buyers disliked the taste
The price was raised at the same time as the pack was changed
Shoppers found the brand by the orange-with-straw image, which was removed
The new pack was withdrawn from many stores for a labelling error
questions.why: Buying behaviour depended on a visual cue.

questions.q: A participant said shoppers had an emotional bond with the old orange. The professor called it instead:
options: Buying behaviour: a learned habit of search
Brand equity built over many years
Representativeness of the category
Mental accounting for a daily habit
questions.why: Right process, wrong label.

questions.q: Which research tools does the slide recommend to avoid a Tropicana-type failure?
options: Price surveys among shoppers leaving the store
Shelf flash recall tests, eye tracking and A/B testing
Focus groups alone, held before the launch
Interviews with the company's own sales force
questions.why: Test how people actually find and choose products.

questions.q: Why can FMCG companies usually afford longer research than technology companies?
options: They have bigger research budgets
They face fewer competitors
Regulators require longer testing
Their products have longer life cycles
questions.why: Tech features are copied within months.

questions.q: Which factor points towards pricing a new product HIGH?
options: The category is habitual and early share matters
Abundant spare capacity
Competitors can copy quickly, so R&D must be recovered fast
The goal is maximum volume
questions.why: Also a deliberate response to capacity constraints.

questions.q: A candy weighs more than rivals. The professor's view on using weight to justify a higher price was that:
options: A heavier candy always justifies a higher price, whatever buyers notice
Customers rarely perceive small weight differences unless the company communicates them
Weight has no bearing on price in a category bought for pleasure
Charging more for extra weight is not permitted for packaged sweets
questions.why: An unperceived benefit cannot carry a price.

questions.q: Why might a new low-priced candy avoid TV advertising at launch?
options: Low absolute margins make ads inefficient, and availability must be secured first
Television advertising of sweets to children is not permitted
Candies, being impulse purchases, never benefit from advertising
Competitors would have complained to the advertising regulator
questions.why: A customer who cannot find an advertised product rarely asks a third time.

questions.q: Involvement in a purchase rises mainly with:
options: The number of brands available in the category
The height of the shelf on which it is displayed
Perceived risk: economic, psychological or performance
The volume of advertising in the category
questions.why: Low risk means low involvement.

questions.q: Clothes that are inexpensive but carry worry about what others will think involve mainly:
options: Economic risk
Performance risk
No risk
Psychological risk
questions.why: The concern is social judgement.

questions.q: "Does your toothpaste contain salt?" is an attempt to:
options: Lower the price of a product buyers see as a commodity
Raise consumer involvement in a low-involvement category
Reposition toothpaste as a luxury for wealthy buyers
Enter a new market of people who do not brush at all
questions.why: Involved buyers become loyal and pay more.

questions.q: Low-involvement categories benefit greatly from advertising because:
options: Buyers choose what they recall at the point of purchase
Buyers compare features carefully before choosing
Margins are high enough to pay for heavy advertising
Products differ greatly and buyers need information
questions.why: Out of sight, out of mind.

questions.q: According to the professor, a lasting advantage for a copyable candy comes mainly from:
options: Patents and trademarks that stop others copying the product
A steady stream of new flavours, which is enough on its own
Heavy television advertising that keeps the brand in mind
Service to the retail channel: frequent visits and no stock-outs
questions.why: Shelf space is the retailer's scarcest resource.

questions.q: A shopkeeper starts stocking a copycat candy mainly when:
options: The copy is cheaper by a rupee and customers ask for it
The copy comes in a better-looking pack and jar
The original is out of stock when customers ask for it
A festival raises the demand for sweets of all kinds
questions.why: A stock-out gives him a reason to give space to a rival.

questions.q: Selling candy in bulk packs and through online and modern-trade channels is which Ansoff strategy?
options: Market penetration
Product development
Market development
Diversification
questions.why: Existing product, existing market, more accessible.

questions.q: A candy brand launching a mango drink is classed by the professor as:
options: Market penetration: existing product, existing market
Diversification: new product, new market
Product development: new product, existing market
Market development: existing product, new market
questions.why: New consumers, price point and competitors; high risk, high reward.

questions.q: Segmentation divides the market into groups that are:
options: Roughly equal in size, so that each can be served at the same cost
Defined only by demographic variables such as age, gender and income
Relatively homogeneous within, with respect to needs, characteristics or behaviour
Made up only of current customers, since others cannot be studied
questions.why: Alike inside, different outside; actual and potential customers.

questions.q: Segmentation improves efficiency mainly by:
options: Doing away with differences that do not affect buying
Designing a separate strategy for every customer
Raising prices for every segment
Increasing the number of segments
questions.why: Irrelevant differences are dropped, so each segment gets one offering.

questions.q: According to the slide, segmentation improves effectiveness through all of the following EXCEPT:
options: A more targeted marketing mix
Increased customer satisfaction
Higher customer lifetime value
A single offering for the whole market
questions.why: A single offering for all is mass marketing: the opposite of segmentation.

questions.q: An AC maker considers pink units for women and blue for men. The professor's view was that:
options: Gender is the best basis for segmenting air conditioners
Gender is not meaningful here; room size and usage matter more
Colour is the attribute AC buyers care about most
Air conditioners cannot usefully be segmented at all
questions.why: A variable earns a segment only if it changes what people buy.

questions.q: "Style-conscious, risk-taker, fun-loving" are examples of which base?
options: Demographic
Behavioural
Psychographic
Geographic
questions.why: Lifestyle and personality variables.

questions.q: User status, usage rate, channel usage and loyalty status are:
options: Behavioural variables
Psychographic variables
Demographic variables
Value-based variables
questions.why: Behaviour within the product category.

questions.q: Colgate's whitening, sensitive and anti-cavity variants are an example of:
options: Geographic segmentation by region
Value-based (need-based) segmentation
Demographic segmentation by age
Mass marketing with one product
questions.why: Each variant serves a different need.

questions.q: The generic approach recommended in class is to:
options: Apply all five bases at once, so that nothing is missed
Start with geography, and add no other variable after it
Use demographics alone, because they are easy to observe
Start with value-based segmentation, then profile the segments
questions.why: Needs first; then who is in each segment, so the 4Ps can be designed.

questions.q: Why is profiling a value-based segment necessary?
options: Profiling removes the need for any further research on the segment
Profiling makes the segment larger by adding similar customers
Without knowing who is in the segment you cannot decide price, place or promotion
Profiling is needed only when the segment is in a business market
questions.why: Media, ad casting, price points and outlets all depend on the profile.

questions.q: Promotion, as the professor defined it, is mainly:
options: Product placement on shelves
Advertising and sales promotion
Choosing distributors
Setting the list price
questions.why: Placement is a small part; ads and sales promotion are the bulk.

questions.q: Marketers use demographics often because they are:
options: Easily visible and observable
The most predictive of all variables
Required by regulators
Always value-based
questions.why: A shopkeeper can see who buys; that ease drives their use.

questions.q: Value-based segmentation is used less than its usefulness suggests mainly because it:
options: Cannot be applied to business markets
Ignores what customers actually need
Usually needs research into customer motivations
Gives segments that are too large
questions.why: It often starts with qualitative research, which costs time and money.

questions.q: In business markets, industry, firm size and ownership are called:
options: Psychographics
Benefits sought
Buying approach
Firmographics
questions.why: The business-market equivalent of demographics.

questions.q: Hillrom found that segmenting hospitals by number of beds was weak because:
options: The bed counts it used were out of date and often inaccurate, so segments were wrongly drawn
Buying behaviour, not size, separated customers: 50- and 250-bed facilities fell in one segment
Large hospitals had stopped buying equipment and were leasing it from other suppliers
Size gave it too few segments to justify the cost of a separate sales force for each
questions.why: Key and prime customers differed in decision makers and purchase drivers.

questions.q: After Hillrom realigned its sales force to key and prime segments, operating income per employee rose by about:
options: 4 to 5 times
questions.why: Revenue per employee rose 11%; operating income per employee 51%.

questions.q: In cluster analysis, the similarity between two respondents is commonly measured by:
options: The correlation between their incomes
The gap between their ages in years
How recently each of them last bought
Euclidean distance between their ratings
questions.why: Square the differences on each variable, add, take the square root.

questions.q: R1 rates three variables (6, 6, 5) and R3 rates them (7, 7, 5). Their Euclidean distance is:
In k-means clustering, k is:
options: The number of clusters the analyst specifies
A number the software finds at the end
The number of variables that are rated
The number of respondents surveyed
questions.why: The analyst asks for, say, 3 clusters; the algorithm assigns and reassigns.

questions.q: A customer appears in two clusters after a segmentation exercise. This means:
options: The segmentation is especially rich, since it captures mixed needs
The exercise has not been done well: segments should not overlap
The customer is a heavy user who needs a segment of his own
The software used k-means, which places some customers twice
questions.why: Good segmentation produces mutually exclusive groups.

questions.q: In a preference-based segmentation chart, the 0% line represents:
options: The rating of the least important variable
The firm's own score on each variable
The average rating of all respondents
A rating of zero importance to everyone
questions.why: Bars show how far each segment sits above or below the average.

questions.q: Segment compatibility refers to:
options: The segment's size, growth and usage, which decide how much it can deliver
How well the firm's chosen segments fit together under a single brand
The lifetime value that a typical customer in the segment will bring
The company's ability to create superior value for the segment relative to competitors
questions.why: Attractiveness asks what the segment is worth; compatibility asks if we can win it.

questions.q: A candy launched in only one flavour is, in SWOT terms:
options: A threat
A weakness
An opportunity
A strength
questions.why: It is internal to the company; threats come from outside.

questions.q: Mountain Dew targeting adventure seekers is an example of:
options: Demographic segmentation
Geographic segmentation
Firmographic segmentation
Psychographic segmentation
questions.why: Adventure seeking is a lifestyle trait.

questions.q: Titan created Fastrack as a separate brand mainly to:
options: Target young buyers while minimising overlap with Titan's own customers
Offer Titan's watches at lower prices without a new name
Enter the business market for corporate gifting of watches
Replace the Titan brand, which was seen as old-fashioned
questions.why: Brands in one portfolio must not cannibalise each other.

questions.q: Madura Garments' brands are separated mainly by:
options: Region and city size
Gender and age group
Occupation and career stage
Fabric and colour
questions.why: Interview (Peter England), mid-level (Van Heusen), corner office (Louis Philippe), smart casual (Allen Solly).

questions.q: Hero launched Pleasure in 2006 mainly to:
options: Enter the motorcycle market, where it was weak
Take on Honda's Activa by targeting women
Target rural men who needed a sturdy scooter
Replace Maestro, whose sales had flattened
questions.why: "Why should boys have all the fun?" (gender-based targeting).

questions.q: Which was NOT a reason the class gave for Bic for Her's failure?
options: It stereotyped women with a "for her" label
Pens are utilitarian and the colour added little value
The ink was a different, inferior formula
It cost about twice as much for a coloured casing
questions.why: The ink was the same blue or black; only the casing changed.

questions.q: The professor's caution on the product life cycle was that it applies best:
options: At the sub-category level, such as black-and-white TVs
To every individual brand, whatever its category
To services, which age faster than products
To luxury goods, which follow fashion cycles
questions.why: A brand's plateau may be a competitive problem to diagnose, not the end of its life.

questions.q: Gap and JCPenney illustrate the risk of:
options: Ignoring cluster analysis when choosing a target segment
Running too few brands to cover every kind of shopper
Pricing too low to pay for a new store layout
Chasing new segments at the cost of loyal existing customers
questions.why: Both strategies alienated the core customer and the leaders were removed.

questions.q: An ethnic-wear brand for women launching menswear would be classed by the professor as:
options: Diversification: new product, new market, non-transferable skills
Market penetration: the brand's existing shoppers would buy it
Product development: a new product for the existing market
Market development: the existing product for a new market
questions.why: Men's tailoring needs different skills; the market is new too.

questions.q: The pregnancy-test maker split buyers into "hopefuls" and "fearfuls". This is:
options: Demographic segmentation
Value-based segmentation
Geographic segmentation
Firmographic segmentation
questions.why: The segments differ in the result, the value, they want.

questions.q: Which segment was priced higher, and why?
options: Fearfuls, because they want to avoid a clinic visit
Both equal, to avoid discrimination
Fearfuls, because they buy more often
Hopefuls, because it is a planned, wished-for purchase
questions.why: For fearfuls it is a grudge purchase, so they seek the lowest price.

questions.q: Selling the same test under two names works only if:
options: Both packs look identical, so that buyers trust the cheaper one as well
The price is the same for both, so that neither segment feels cheated
The two segments value it differently and are kept apart by name, pack and placement
Both versions are sold online only, where shelves cannot be compared
questions.why: If segments meet both products side by side, the strategy is exposed.

questions.q: Positioning is best defined as:
options: Advertising the product widely, so that as many target customers as possible become aware of it and of its benefits
The marketer's effort to occupy a clear, distinctive and attractive place in target customers' minds relative to competitors
Placing the product on the right shelf, in the right stores, where target customers will look for it and its rivals
Setting a price that tells target customers where the product stands in relation to competing products
questions.why: Advertising is a means; the image in the mind is the end.

questions.q: The professor's formula for positioning is:
options: Target segment + differentiation
Price + quality
Product + promotion
Segmentation + targeting
questions.why: Know whom you serve and what you offer them that rivals do not.

questions.q: A perceptual map built from a survey requires you to know:
options: Every competitor's cost of production
The firm's market share in each segment
The two attributes customers use most in the category
The discount rate used for the category
questions.why: Customers rate brands on those attributes and the averages are plotted.

questions.q: Subway's entry into fast food illustrates:
options: Extending an established brand into a new category
Mass marketing with one standard offer for everyone
Repositioning a brand whose image had gone stale
Finding a desirable vacant space on a perceptual map
questions.why: Rivals were tasty but unhealthy; Subway claimed tasty and healthy.

questions.q: Multidimensional scaling asks respondents mainly:
options: How much they would pay
How similar pairs of brands are
Their age and income
Which ad they recall
questions.why: Similarity ratings alone are enough; the software builds the map.

questions.q: In MDS, who names the dimensions of the output map?
options: The researcher, using experience or expert input
The software, from the similarity ratings
The respondents, while rating the pairs
The brands, through their advertising
questions.why: The algorithm places brands; interpretation is the analyst's job.

questions.q: Usually an MDS output is requested in two dimensions because:
options: Statistical software cannot produce more than two
Customers use only one attribute, plus price
A third dimension always repeats the first two
It is easiest to interpret, and two dimensions usually stand out
questions.why: Three-dimensional outputs are hard to read.

questions.q: Goodyear's wet-traction tyre story shows that:
options: An innovation always shifts customers' perception in time
Tread life does not matter to people who buy tyres
A real product advantage may not register in customers' minds
Tyres are a commodity that cannot be positioned
questions.why: Customers rated it no differently; the positioning had not translated.

questions.q: In the three-circle framework, your point of difference is the area where:
options: Your offering meets customer needs and the competitor's does not
All three circles overlap
The competitor's offering meets needs and yours does not
Your offering does not meet any need
questions.why: Area B. The three-way overlap is points of parity.

questions.q: A weight-loss drug that works as well as rivals but causes no gastric trouble. Its point of difference is:
options: Its effectiveness
Fewer side effects
Its price
Its category
questions.why: Effectiveness is parity; fewer side effects is the difference.

questions.q: Renault Kwid broke the assumption that budget car buyers want only mileage by segmenting on:
options: Geography: small towns against large cities
Demographics: income bands of first-time buyers
Psychographics: aspirational features for young buyers
Behaviour: how many kilometres a buyer drives
questions.why: It offered SUV-like styling and bigger-car features at a low price.

questions.q: Chik shampoo's sachets targeted rural consumers who did not use shampoo. This targeting used:
options: Psychographic segmentation
Firmographics
Gender
Behavioural segmentation: non-users
questions.why: Like the Nano's two-wheeler owners, the target was defined by non-use.

questions.q: Ratan Tata said the Nano "got wrongly positioned". The best explanation is that:
options: Tata's own advertisements called it the cheapest car in the world
Media attention to its record low price fixed the image, contrary to the intended position
It turned out to be too expensive for the families it was aimed at
It was deliberately aimed at existing car owners as a second car
questions.why: Its ads stressed quality and robustness; the coverage stressed price.

questions.q: You can best judge a company's intended positioning from:
options: Its share price and results
Its competitors' advertising
Newspaper and TV headlines
Its own communication and advertising
questions.why: Intended position shows in what the brand says about itself.

questions.q: Volkswagen's Phaeton failed mainly because:
options: Buyers of ultra-luxury cars did not want to be associated with a people's-car brand, and it was sold from the same showrooms
It lacked the features and finish that buyers of ultra-luxury cars expect, and reviewers said so at launch
It was priced well above rival luxury cars and had no dealer network of its own to support it
It was launched only in India, where the market for ultra-luxury cars is still very small
questions.why: Positioning plus a misaligned channel.

questions.q: On a price-quality map, which move is hardest for a brand?
options: Downscale, offering a cheaper line under the same name
Sideways, adding a variant at the same price point
Upscale, offering a premium line under the same name
None; all moves are equally hard for a brand
questions.why: Customers accept a premium brand going down more readily than a mass brand going up.

questions.q: Toyota entered the ultra-premium market with:
options: A sub-brand, Toyota Lexus
A separate brand, Lexus
A price cut on the Camry
A new channel, like Nexa
questions.why: A new name avoided the upscale-stretch problem.

questions.q: The three key elements of a positioning statement are:
options: Product, price, place and promotion, each stated in one line for the target
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, as customers see them
Who (target), what (point of difference and frame of reference), why (reason to believe)
Segment, target and position, written out in the order they were decided
questions.why: Who, what and why, per the slide.

questions.q: A positioning statement is mainly:
options: An internal document that aligns everyone on what the brand stands for
An advertising slogan written for customers to remember
A legal filing that protects the brand's name and logo
A price list that shows where the brand sits in its market
questions.why: It can also be the basis for an agency brief.

questions.q: In "Among snackers, Snickers is the brand of candy bar that satisfies your hunger because it is packed with peanuts", the frame of reference is:
options: Snackers
Satisfies your hunger
Packed with peanuts
Candy bar
questions.why: The frame is the competitive category the brand benchmarks against.

questions.q: In the Gatorade statement, the frame of reference is:
options: Water
Soft drinks
Energy drinks
Athletes
questions.why: "Hydrates, replenishes and refuels in ways water can't."

questions.q: Why might Gatorade not state a reason to believe?
options: It has no reason to believe, since water hydrates just as well
Much of the refuelling comes from sugar, which carries negative connotations
Positioning statements never include one for a sports drink
Electrolytes may not be mentioned on the label of a drink
questions.why: Highlighting only part of the reason, or sugar, may not look good.

questions.q: Tropicana changing its packaging is best described as:
options: Repositioning
Brand extension
Diversification
Rebranding
questions.why: A new look is not a new image in customers' minds.

questions.q: Starbucks adding sandwiches and tea is, in the professor's view:
options: Repositioning itself as a food company with coffee on the side
Diversification into an unrelated business with new customers
A growth move; it still wants to be seen as a premium coffee outlet
Rebranding, since the look of its stores changed with the menu
questions.why: Adding products is not repositioning unless the brand's meaning changes.

questions.q: Cadbury Dairy Milk's move to "kuch meetha ho jaaye" repositioned the brand mainly by:
options: Changing the communication and frame of reference to traditional sweets
Changing the chocolate's recipe to taste more like a sweet
Cutting the price to match that of traditional sweets
Selling through sweet shops instead of grocery stores
questions.why: A communication-only repositioning that widened it to adults and occasions.

questions.q: Fair & Lovely's multipurpose relaunch lost about 20% share in two months mainly because:
options: The new cream did not work as well as the old one on dark spots
Competitors cut their prices as soon as the relaunch was announced
The name was changed to Glow & Lovely at the same time as the pack
Rural customers had not seen the new ads and thought the changed pack was fake
questions.why: Repositioning must be communicated to every customer group.

questions.q: A launch positioned for "anyone, anytime" but priced at about Rs. 50, with one variant and an energy-themed name, illustrates:
options: Strong mass positioning that needed only a larger advertising budget
Confused positioning: the 4Ps contradict the intended mass position
A sound niche strategy let down by the choice of retail outlets
A successful repositioning from an energy drink to a soft drink
questions.why: Mass needs low price, variety and broad appeal; every P must agree.

questions.q: The word "brand" comes from the Old Norse brandr, meaning:
options: To sell
To own
To trade
To burn
questions.why: Owners burned marks on cattle to tell them apart.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the views of a brand on the class slide?
options: A customer experience represented by images and ideas
The legal registration of a company's name
A promise made by a firm to its customers
A network of associations in consumer memory
questions.why: The three views stress experience, promise and associations.

questions.q: A queue outside a store for a one-day 70% discount mainly shows:
options: The power of the discount, not the brand
Strong loyalty to the brand
High brand equity in fashion
The pull of ingredient branding
questions.why: A real fan pays more, in money and time, without a discount.

questions.q: Harley-Davidson is called the poster child of branding mainly because:
options: It spends more on advertising than any other motorcycle maker in the world
It keeps its prices below those of Japanese motorcycles of the same size
It has never been in financial trouble since it was founded in 1903
It built intense loyalty with little advertising, its employees and riders carrying the brand
questions.why: Owners' rides, HOG, even tattoos, and licensing income.

questions.q: Brand management as a function is traced to a 1931 memo by:
options: Philip Kotler, the author
Peter Drucker, the thinker
Neil McElroy of P&G
Al Ries, the consultant
questions.why: He asked for a dedicated team for Camay, which competed with P&G's own Ivory.

questions.q: Johnson & Johnson's handling of the 1982 Tylenol poisonings is remembered because it:
options: Recalled the product nationwide and relaunched with tamper-proof packaging
Blamed its distributors and withdrew only the affected batches
Changed the brand name and relaunched it as a new product
Cut the price sharply to win customers back after the scare
questions.why: The first major recall; trust in the brand brought it back.

questions.q: When Maggi was off the shelves in 2015, the main effect was that:
options: Yippee took most of its share permanently
Consumers lost trust in the noodle category as a whole
Pasta sales replaced noodle sales exactly
Maggi never returned
questions.why: Maggi came back to about 60% share; trust sat with the brand.

questions.q: In the blind beer test, when brand names were hidden:
options: All six brands still tasted clearly different
Guinness could not be told from the others
Five mass brands tasted alike; only Guinness stood apart
Drinkers preferred the cheapest of the six
questions.why: Brands shape perception, even of taste.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four challenges (Cs) in building a strong brand?
options: Cash
Contemporary
Clutter
Channels
questions.why: Cash, contemporary, clutter and consistency.

questions.q: The cash challenge arises because brand-building costs are:
options: Uncertain and in the future, while benefits are immediate
Certain and immediate, while benefits are uncertain and in the future
Tax-free
Always small
questions.why: Managers with short tenures prefer short-term measures.

questions.q: Running sales promotions too often tends to:
options: Strengthen the brand by reminding buyers of it often
Raise the price premium the brand can command
Cut through the clutter of rival advertising
Teach customers to buy the promotion, not the brand
questions.why: Later, nobody will pay full price.

questions.q: Kodak's decline is best explained by:
options: Failing to stay contemporary: it invented digital but protected film
Weak distribution outside the United States and Europe
Too many brand extensions that diluted the Kodak name
A fighter brand that cannibalised its premium film
questions.why: It sat on its own patents for fear of hurting film.

questions.q: Lux has stayed relevant for decades mainly by:
options: Changing its core product often
Cutting prices
Changing its celebrity endorsers
Becoming a house of brands
questions.why: From Leela Chitnis onwards, a succession of heroines.

questions.q: Olay's change from "Oil of Olay" was made because:
options: The oil it contained was banned in several of its main markets
"Oil" suggested stickiness rather than cosmetics, and the brand looked dated
P&G had sold the brand and the new owner wanted a new name
It was being turned into an ingredient brand for other creams
questions.why: Dropping the word and refreshing the look repositioned it.

questions.q: Lucky Strike's "It's toasted" in Mad Men illustrates:
options: Delivering the same promise at every touch point
Promoting a branded component inside a product
Breaking the clutter by being first to claim something
Cutting the number of brands in a portfolio
questions.why: Everyone toasted tobacco; only one brand said so.

questions.q: Only about what share of the 1955 Fortune 500 was still on the list in 2017?
questions.why: About 60 companies: evidence of how hard consistency is.

questions.q: Launching new flavours of an existing biscuit under the same name is a:
options: Category extension
New brand
Fighter brand
Line extension
questions.why: Existing name, existing category.

questions.q: Dove moving from soap into body lotion is a:
options: Category extension
Line extension
Store brand
Ingredient brand
questions.why: Existing name, new category.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of brand extension?
options: It saves time and money
It may dilute the parent brand
It aids awareness
It reduces risk for customers
questions.why: Also cannibalisation and losing the chance to reach a new segment with a new brand.

questions.q: A fighter brand meant to battle low-priced rivals is best launched:
options: Under the parent's name, to borrow its trust and awareness
As a store brand, sold through one retail chain only
Only online, where the parent brand is not available
Under a new name, to limit cannibalisation and protect the parent
questions.why: A new name keeps the parent's image and customers safe.

questions.q: Crystal Pepsi failed mainly because:
options: It was priced well above ordinary colas in the same pack
It contained no caffeine and tasted too weak for cola drinkers
"Clear cola" confused buyers: cola is associated with brown
Coca-Cola held a patent that kept it out of most stores
questions.why: The extension broke a core category association.

questions.q: Coca-Cola's Tab Clear, launched next to Crystal Pepsi, is described as a:
options: Kamikaze strategy: hurting the rival at a cost to itself
Fighter brand that succeeded in protecting Coke's core
Line extension of Coke that widened its appeal
Store brand made for one large retail chain
questions.why: Both products failed and Tab was damaged.

questions.q: Bic's lighters and razors succeeded while its perfume failed because:
options: Perfume is seen as a stationery product, which Bic's buyers do not want from it
The perfume was priced too high for a brand known for affordable products
Lighters and razors are ingredient brands, while perfume is sold on its own
Bic's "affordable, disposable" association fits lighters and razors but not hedonic perfume
questions.why: Fit comes from all the parent's associations, not just its category.

questions.q: Pond's toothpaste failed mainly because:
options: Pond's had too little awareness outside cities
Pond's means external beauty, not oral care
It was priced too low to look effective
It cannibalised Pond's own cold cream
questions.why: Its powder and cream fit; toothpaste did not.

questions.q: Honda City, Hyundai i20 and Cadbury Dairy Milk are examples of:
options: Individual branding
Ingredient branding
Sub-branding
Store brands
questions.why: Parent and new name share emphasis.

questions.q: P&G's Tide, Ariel and Pampers reflect which firm-level strategy?
options: House of brands
Branded house
Ingredient branding
Private labels
questions.why: Individual brands; the parent stays in the background.

questions.q: Godrej, Dell and Virgin reflect which strategy?
options: House of brands (individual branding)
Branded house (corporate branding)
Endorser branding (a light parent name)
Fighter branding (a low-price flanker)
questions.why: The firm's name is on almost every offering.

questions.q: "Intel Inside" on a laptop is an example of:
options: A private label
A fighter brand
Line extension
Ingredient branding
questions.why: A branded component inside another branded product is promoted.

questions.q: A brand has a price of Rs. 100, variable cost Rs. 70 and allocated fixed cost Rs. 40 per unit. Dropping it would:
options: Save Rs. 10 per unit, the loss it shows after fixed costs
Save Rs. 40 per unit, the fixed cost allocated to it
Lose Rs. 30 per unit of contribution toward fixed costs
Change nothing, since price covers variable cost
questions.why: Contribution is positive; the fixed costs remain anyway.

questions.q: A hospital brand known for emergency care opens a cancer unit. The main brand risk the professor highlighted is:
options: Cannibalisation of its emergency patients by the new unit
Dilution of the parent brand if the new unit disappoints
Confusion with ingredient brands used in treatment
Competition from private-label hospital chains
questions.why: The segments do not substitute; image damage is the risk.

questions.q: "Positioning is not what you do to a product; it is what you do to the mind of the prospect." This line is from:
options: Peter Drucker
Daniel Kahneman
Ries and Trout
Neil McElroy
questions.why: Positioning is the image, not the advertising that creates it.

questions.q: How does behaviour differ from psychographics as a basis of segmentation?
options: Behaviour is how a person acts within this product category; psychographics describe the person's wider lifestyle
Behaviour describes the person's wider lifestyle; psychographics are how the person acts within this category
Behaviour is measured by income and occupation; psychographics by age and where the person lives
They are two names for the same base, one used for consumer markets and one for business markets
questions.why: A party-goer is a lifestyle; brushing twice a day is behaviour in the category.

questions.q: In the multiplex popcorn example (small about Rs. 600, medium about Rs. 750, large about Rs. 800) which tub is the decoy?
options: The small
The large
None; all three are meant to sell
The medium
questions.why: It costs nearly as much as the large and gives much less, so the large looks obvious.

questions.q: Fast fashion was the professor's example of a category where:
options: Life cycles are so short that long research is not possible
Research can take as long as it needs, since designs last for years
Designs are protected by law, so nobody is able to copy them
Customers' tastes change so slowly that research is not needed
questions.why: A design seen on the runway is in the stores within days.

questions.q: In the Snickers positioning statement, the point of difference is that it:
options: Tastes better than other candy bars
Satisfies your hunger
Costs less than a meal
Is packed with peanuts
questions.why: Peanuts are the reason to believe; hunger is the difference.

questions.q: According to its launch communication, the Tata Nano's intended target was:
options: Existing car owners in big cities looking for a cheap second car for short trips
College students and young professionals wanting a sporty, stylish first car
Taxi and fleet operators who needed the lowest running cost per kilometre
Families without a car: two-wheeler owners in smaller towns moving up to four wheels
questions.why: The intended positioning is read from the company's own advertising.

questions.q: A participant defined positioning as "placement". The professor pointed out that placement means:
options: The same thing as positioning: the two words can be used interchangeably
The choice of which segment to serve, which is properly called targeting
Shelf placement, or product placement in films: each a technical term of its own
The price band in which a product is placed relative to its competitors
questions.why: Positioning is the image in the customer's mind.

questions.q: Besides the brand's "people's car" image, what else hurt Volkswagen's Phaeton?
options: It was sold from the same showrooms as Volkswagen's cheaper cars
It lacked the features that rival ultra-luxury cars already offered
It was priced far above its rivals, with no finance on offer
It was never advertised, so buyers did not know that it existed
questions.why: An ultra-luxury buyer expects to be treated differently.

questions.q: As told in class, about 80% of The Economist's readers chose web only before a print-only option was added. Afterwards, about:
options: 80% still chose web only
50% chose print only
90% chose web-plus-print
70% chose web-plus-print
questions.why: Print only at the same $125 made web-plus-print look like a free gift.

questions.q: A toothpaste maker urging people to brush twice a day is using which growth strategy?
options: Product development
Market penetration
Market development
Diversification
questions.why: More usage of the existing product by the existing market.

questions.q: How many segments did the professor suggest a cluster analysis should usually end with?
options: One or two
Eight to ten
Three or four
As many as there are respondents
questions.why: Beyond five, segments become small and strategies too many to be efficient.

questions.q: Which Madura Garments brand was aimed at smart-casual workplaces and introduced the idea of Friday dressing?
options: Allen Solly
Peter England
Van Heusen
Louis Philippe
questions.why: The four brands are separated by occupation and career stage.

questions.q: The bank advertisement shown in class asked viewers to see a savings rate of 6% against 4% as:
options: 2% more, not 50% extra
50% extra, not 2% more
A loss of 4%
A discount of 33%
questions.why: The same difference, reframed to look larger.

questions.q: Marketers lean heavily on behavioural segmentation today mainly because:
options: Behaviour is the easiest thing to see in a shop
It needs no data at all
Regulators require it
Firms are sitting on large amounts of customer data
questions.why: Demographics are popular because they are visible; behaviour because the data exist.

questions.q: Your brand's sales have flattened while the category is still growing. According to the class, you should:
options: Assume the product has matured and launch a replacement at once
Withdraw the product before its decline starts to hurt the brand
Diagnose your own strategy: the problem is the brand, not the life cycle
Cut advertising to protect margins until the category stops growing
questions.why: The life cycle applies best at the sub-category level, not to a single brand's mistakes.

questions.q: Mirrors in clothing stores and screens beside a billing queue apply the lesson of the Houston baggage claim, which is that:
options: A stated wait becomes an anchor
Occupied time is not felt as waiting time
Buyers prefer gains to reduced losses
Shoppers pick the middle option
questions.why: Time, like money, is booked into separate mental accounts.

questions.q: Walmart paid about 16 billion dollars for control of a loss-making Flipkart. The professor used this to show that:
options: The customer base, like the brand, is an intangible asset worth valuing
Loss-making firms are usually overvalued by buyers from abroad
Land, plant and machinery explain most of an online retailer's value
The cost of acquiring customers does not matter in e-commerce
questions.why: If customers are assets, a firm needs a way to value them: hence the interest in CLV.

questions.q: A hypermarket adds "maximum 4 per customer" to a modest discount on cookies, and shoppers buy more. The limit works as:
options: A decoy that makes another pack look better
A negative frame
An anchor for how many to buy
A separate mental account
questions.why: The professor bought four; without the line she would have bought two or three.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a measure of segment attractiveness?
options: The size of the segment and its rate of growth
How much the segment's members use the product
The lifetime value of the segment's customers
The company's strengths relative to competitors
questions.why: That is compatibility: whether we can serve the segment better than rivals can.

questions.q: Old Spice was mentioned in class as an example of a brand that:
options: Failed because it segmented by gender and stereotyped its buyers
Must attract younger buyers without alienating its ageing loyal base
Lost its loyal customers by repositioning as a higher-priced brand
Was withdrawn after a recall and never recovered its market share
questions.why: A quieter version of the dilemma that cost two retail chief executives their jobs.

questions.q: Kellogg's Special K breakfast sandwich did not work because:
options: Customers could not connect a sausage, egg and cheese sandwich with a weight-loss brand
Rural customers had not seen the new advertising and took the changed pack for a fake
It was sold from the same shelves as the cereal and took sales away from it
Its price was set too low for a brand that customers had come to see as premium
questions.why: Moving far from what the brand stands for usually fails.

questions.q: In a habitual category, where buyers stay with the taste they are used to, the factor "habit" points towards:
options: A higher price, to recover R&D
Skipping the test market
Selling only online
A lower price, to win share early
questions.why: Whoever wins the habit first tends to keep it.

questions.q: A perceptual map shows a marketer two things. They are:
options: The brand's market share in each segment, and how that share has changed over time
The price each brand charges, and the cost at which each brand is produced
Whether customers see the brand where it was intended, and whether a desirable space is vacant
Which advertisements customers remember, and which of them they liked the most
questions.why: Subway found its vacant space in healthy-and-tasty fast food.

questions.q: When Maggi returned to the shelves after being withdrawn in 2015, it:
options: Climbed back quickly to about 60% of the market
Never recovered beyond about 10% of the market
Was relaunched under a new name and a new pack
Lost its lead for good to another noodle brand
questions.why: The brand, not the category, held the trust.

questions.q: When Harley-Davidson was owned by AMF, what went wrong?
options: The company stopped making motorcycles and moved into licensed merchandise
Production was pushed up and the Harley name played down, which riders disliked
Advertising was tripled, which made the brand look ordinary to its riders
The owners' club was closed down and the company's dealers were replaced
questions.why: After the buy-back, Harley competed on legacy rather than on Japanese terms.

questions.q: After Hero launched Pleasure for women in 2006, its share of the scooter market:
options: Fell from 16.9% to 9.8%
Stayed at about 19%
Rose from 9.8% to 16.9%
Rose from 15% to 85%
questions.why: When that growth flattened, Hero launched Maestro for men.

questions.q: Sleepy Owl raised the click-through rates of its advertisements by:
options: Doubling its advertising budget and moving all of it to social media
Hiring a film star whose image matched what the brand wanted to say
Showing a struck-through higher price beside the offer price in every ad
Using the words customers said they valued: low acidity, great aroma, smooth taste
questions.why: Survey answers were turned straight into advertising copy.

questions.q: Why can a blind taste test mislead a company about a well-loved brand?
options: Tasters cannot reliably tell a sweeter drink from a less sweet one in small sips
Real buying happens with the brand visible, and knowing the brand changes the answer
Blind tests are always run with too few people to give a result worth trusting
Taste plays almost no part in the choice of a soft drink once the price is known
questions.why: Brand loyalty showed up only when people knew what they were drinking.

questions.q: People asked to write down the last digits of an unrelated number before pricing a pen quoted higher prices when their digits were higher. This shows that:
options: People with higher numbers are richer
Pens are bought as luxuries
A loss frame raises prices
Even an irrelevant number can act as an anchor
questions.why: The number had nothing to do with the product, and it still pulled the estimate.

questions.q: In the US lawsuit over burgers that looked bigger in advertisements than in real life, the court:
options: Found for the company: a reasonable person understands advertising images
Fined the company and ordered it to withdraw the advertisements
Banned the use of photographs of food in restaurant advertising
Ordered the company to make its burgers match the size shown
questions.why: The buyer is expected to interpret advertising sensibly.

questions.q: Match the route used to break the clutter: Nivea's blue tin, Amul's butter girl, Nirma's jingle.
options: Mascot, packaging, logo
Logo, design, packaging
Packaging, mascot, advertising
Advertising, logo, mascot
questions.why: Differentiation does not always need a new technology.

questions.q: The notes suggest Sleepy Owl's surveys work because they are:
options: Long, and run once a year
Short, frequent and tied to a specific decision
Sent only to people who have never bought
Handled by an agency in another city
questions.why: Each answer changes something customers can see.

questions.q: A challenger whose product does not look like the prototype the category leader has established must:
options: Price well below the leader until customers switch
Withdraw, because a category's prototype cannot change
Spend heavily to make customers see it differently
Adopt a name that sounds like the leader's name
questions.why: Borrowing a category cue is quick; breaking the prototype is costly.

questions.q: An ethnic-wear brand already sells a small kids' line and decides to expand it. On the Ansoff matrix this is:
options: Market penetration, because the line already exists
Product development, because kids' wear is a new product
Market development, because children are a new market
Diversification, because product and market are both new
questions.why: Check what already exists before calling something new.

questions.q: "Every customer touch point is a moment of truth" belongs to which of the four challenges of brand building?
options: Cash
Clutter
Contemporary
Consistency
questions.why: The brand has to deliver its promise at every contact, for decades.

questions.q: Why does watching customers at home reveal things that interviews miss?
options: People stop noticing small nuisances and so never mention them
People deliberately mislead interviewers about what they do
Observation costs far less than interviewing the same people
Interviews can cover only a handful of people at a time
questions.why: P&G's shift was from asking what people want to watching what they do.

questions.q: "15 of the 19 big banks pass the stress test" and "4 of the 19 big banks fail" illustrate:
options: Anchoring: the first number seen sets the scale
Framing: the same fact presented as a gain or as a loss
Availability: what is easily recalled feels likely
Representativeness: judging by fit with a stereotype
questions.why: Identical information, two different impressions.

questions.q: For a hospital known for emergency care opening a cancer unit, the professor leaned towards sub-branding with the parent name prominent because:
options: A new name is always cheaper
Cancer patients would otherwise go to the emergency ward
Endorser branding is not permitted for hospitals
In services, trust matters even more and takes very long to build
questions.why: The risk to manage is dilution, not cannibalisation.

questions.q: With a retention rate of 50%, the probability that a customer is still with the firm in year 3 is:
questions.why: Survival is r to the power t - 1: 1 in year 1, 0.5 in year 2, 0.25 in year 3.

questions.q: Rs. 999 reads as "nine hundred-something" and Rs. 1,000 as "a thousand". This is the:
options: Left-digit effect
Veblen effect
Goldilocks effect
Decoy effect
questions.why: The leftmost digit has the most influence on how a price is read.

questions.q: A survey is best described as a method that is:
options: Qualitative, and about what people do
Qualitative, and about what people say
Quantitative, and about what people do
Quantitative, and about what people say
questions.why: Many respondents, measurable answers, but people may not do what they say.

questions.q: Which of these is repositioning rather than rebranding?
options: A juice brand redesigning its carton and changing the wording on it
A deodorant brand moving its message from seduction to individuality
A company replacing its old logo with a simpler, more modern one
A retail chain repainting its stores and changing its staff uniforms
questions.why: Repositioning tries to create a new image; rebranding changes the look, the logo or the name.

questions.q: Each time a participant offered "market research" or "competitor analysis" as a marketing decision, the professor replied that these are:
options: The most important decisions a marketing manager takes
Decisions that belong to the finance function
Activities that feed decisions: to take what decision?
Part of Place in the 4Ps
questions.why: A plan is a list of choices; research and tracking exist to inform them.

questions.q: Why did Kimberly-Clark sell adult diapers as Depend rather than as an extension of Huggies?
options: Adults would not want a brand associated with toddlers
Huggies was losing share and could not support a new product
The law does not allow one name on products for two age groups
A new name is always cheaper to advertise than an existing one
questions.why: Perceived fit, seen from the customer's side.

questions.q: Within the 4Ps, brand management sits under:
options: Price
Product
Place
Promotion
questions.why: Services, too, are treated as part of Product.

questions.q: Where did the pregnancy-test maker place the version meant for the "fearfuls"?
options: Next to ovulation kits and vitamins
At the pharmacy's billing counter
In the baby-care and nappies aisle
Next to condoms and contraceptives
questions.why: Name, pack and shelf kept the two segments from discovering each other's product.

questions.q: Neil McElroy's 1931 memo asked for a dedicated team because his brand, Camay, was:
options: Being copied by a rival company that had launched a similar-looking soap
Sold in only one region and needed a national sales force in order to grow
Competing against P&G's own flagship soap, Ivory, without resources of its own
About to be withdrawn because its sales had been falling for several years
questions.why: The memo is regarded as the birth certificate of brand management.

questions.q: Research cited in class found that a brand rated 3 out of 5, which falls to 1 after a failure, can end up rated about:
options: 1, whatever the company does
4, if the failure is handled well
3, the same as before
5, in every case
questions.why: Good after-sales handling can turn a failure into loyalty.
