questions.q: A participant argued that the product must come before STP. The professor's reply was that:
options: The broad category is a business decision; the specific product decisions follow the segment and positioning
The product always comes first; segmentation and positioning are worked out after the launch
STP and the product are both decided by the production team before marketing is involved
The order makes no difference so long as the price is set before the product is designed
questions.why: Airbags, features and variants have to serve a target that has already been chosen.

questions.q: Compared with niche positioning, mass positioning usually means:
options: Lower volume, higher margin and stronger appeal to a few
Higher volume and higher margin, with appeal to everyone
Higher volume, lower margin and weaker appeal to any one group
Lower volume and lower margin, with appeal to a small group
questions.why: Something for everyone becomes very appealing to no one.

questions.q: The class said Jio stands for free, cheap plans and freedom. The professor used this to argue that:
options: Jio's name can be extended into any category without risk
Telecom brands cannot be extended beyond telecom services
A brand's associations do not matter in service categories
Those associations would not help a premium education brand
questions.why: Tata's association with trust, by contrast, travels across categories.

questions.q: The changes Tropicana made in its failed relaunch were:
options: A new formula with less sugar, in the same familiar carton as before
Cosmetic: the pack, the logo and the claims; the juice was the same
A higher price and a smaller pack, with no change to the design
A move from cartons to bottles, sold through different retailers
questions.why: Shoppers could no longer find the orange they looked for on the shelf.

questions.q: HMT lost its leadership in watches mainly because:
options: Titan arrived with quartz technology and HMT did not move in time
It raised its prices sharply and lost the gifting market to imports
Its watches were recalled after a quality failure and never returned
It stopped advertising once it had become the default gift
questions.why: Like Kodak, it had the technology but failed to stay contemporary.

questions.q: What made the Gillette Guard right for the Indian market?
options: Twin blades developed with Indian students at MIT, at a premium price
A battery-powered handle that gave a closer shave in poor light
A disposable design sold only through modern retail in large cities
A single blade that rinsed easily with little water, at a low price
questions.why: It was designed after watching men shave at home with a cup of water.

questions.q: Pears was not among the top five soap brands, yet it was kept during portfolio rationalisation because it had:
options: The lowest variable cost
A strong regional base in the south
A strong image with future growth potential
The same positioning as another brand
questions.why: The brand kept for its regional strength was Hamam.

questions.q: Colgate launches a toothpaste for sensitive teeth. Calling it "Colgate Sensitive" rather than giving it a new name means that:
options: More of its sales will come from Colgate's own customers
More of its sales will come from competitors' customers
It cannot be sold in the same shops
It becomes a fighter brand
questions.why: If cannibalisation is the worry, a new name is safer.

questions.q: A company launching a novelty knows it cannot meet demand at a low price. This points towards:
options: A lower price
A higher price
No advertising at any stage
Leaving the market
questions.why: Capacity is one of the factors in the choice between a high and a low launch price.

questions.q: In endorser branding:
options: The parent's name, with a product description, is the only name used
The parent and the new name share roughly equal emphasis on the pack
The new name leads and the parent appears lightly as an endorsement
The parent is kept hidden from customers in all of the communication
questions.why: Equal emphasis is sub-branding; the parent alone is corporate branding.

questions.q: In the three-circle framework, the area where customer needs, your offering and the competitor's offering all overlap holds the:
options: Points of difference
Competitor's points of difference
Unmet needs
Points of parity
questions.why: Parity gets you considered; it gives no reason to choose you.

questions.q: The two attributes tyre buyers mainly look at, in the Goodyear example, were:
options: Price and colour
Tread life and wet traction
Brand name and warranty
Speed rating and noise
questions.why: Goodyear improved wet traction, yet customers rated it no differently.

questions.q: A smart group listing pricing factors from memory forgot distribution altogether. The professor used this to show that:
options: Distribution has little effect on the price a customer pays
Pricing is best left to the finance and accounting team
Memory is a better guide than a framework for experts
A framework is a checklist that stops you missing things
questions.why: Run the same problem through the 5Cs and distribution cannot be forgotten: it has a box.

questions.q: When the class listed variables for segmenting hypermarket shoppers, proximity was left out because:
options: A marketing manager cannot change the store's location
Shoppers do not care how far they travel to a hypermarket
Distance cannot be rated on a scale of one to seven
It is a demographic variable, not a value customers seek
questions.why: Choose variables on which the marketer can act.

questions.q: Store brands are priced lower than national brands, yet retailers earn more on them. Why?
options: They are made from cheaper ingredients than national brands of the same type
Customers are willing to pay a premium for a retailer's own name on the pack
The store's own trust saves brand-building cost, and there are fewer middlemen
National manufacturers subsidise them in return for better shelf space
questions.why: National brands, with their bargaining power, leave retailers thin margins.

questions.q: A new competitor entering the market is, in SWOT terms:
options: A weakness, because it hurts the company
A threat, because it comes from outside the company
A strength, because it enlarges the market
Neither internal nor external
questions.why: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external.

questions.q: A participant noted that luxury brands avoid strike-through prices and bonus packs. The explanation is that:
options: Luxury buyers are far less affected by anchors and frames than ordinary buyers are
Luxury brands are bound by agreements with their retailers never to discount
Those tactics make a price look low, while luxury relies on exclusivity: the Veblen effect
Anchoring and framing have been shown to work only on low-priced products
questions.why: Even so, the snob effect holds only within a range of prices.

questions.q: Why would a caffeine-free drink struggle if it were positioned as an energy drink?
options: One dominant brand defines the category's prototype, and the drink does not fit it
Energy drinks are bought mainly in rural markets, where the brand had no reach
Customers who buy energy drinks actively dislike drinks that contain vitamins
Energy drinks must be priced below soft drinks to sell in any real volume
questions.why: Representativeness again: customers would ask where the energy comes from.

questions.q: A brand leads its communication with "reliable" and "good mileage", which every rival also claims. It is:
options: Using its strongest point of difference in a crowded market
Repositioning itself away from what it stood for earlier
Stating its reason to believe without naming its target
Leading with points of parity, which give no reason to choose it
questions.why: The positioning has to be built on a difference customers value.

questions.q: To decide which branding approach a product uses, the professor advised looking at:
options: How the company names it in advertising, on the front of the pack and in interviews
Which company legally owns the trademark and where it has been registered
Where the product is manufactured and which factory's name is on the pack
How the product is priced compared with the parent brand's other products
questions.why: The boundaries are blurred; judge by emphasis.

questions.q: In the language of Session 1, a bias is:
options: A mental shortcut used to decide quickly
The systematic error that a heuristic produces
A deliberate attempt by a company to mislead
The gap between a product's price and its cost
questions.why: The heuristic is the shortcut; the bias is the predictable mistake it leads to.

questions.q: The first step in deciding whether to extend a brand is to:
options: Check that the factory has spare capacity and that the channel will stock the product
Choose the advertising agency and agree the budget for the launch campaign
Set the price of the new product in line with the parent brand's price
Bring out all the parent brand's associations from customers, not just its product category
questions.why: Bic's "affordable and disposable" mattered more than "stationery".

questions.q: In case analysis, the recommendation "start again with fresh research" was rejected because:
options: Research is rarely useful once a product has already been launched
The case contained no research on which a recommendation could rest
A recommendation must say what to change, using the research already in hand
Only the company, not the analyst, may decide to commission research
questions.why: Name the changes, across all four Ps.

questions.q: An Indian candy brand entering Singapore because of its large Indian population is pursuing:
options: Market development
Market penetration
Product development
Diversification
questions.why: An existing product in a new market: starting where tastes are familiar.

questions.q: A company sold the same tablet at a higher price under a migraine label. Challenged in court, it argued that:
options: The two tablets contained different active ingredients in different strengths
The higher price paid for the extra advertising that the migraine label needed
Customers had asked for a separate product and were willing to pay more for it
The migraine pack carries different dosage information and offers psychological value
questions.why: As the professor recalled, the company won.

questions.q: Told that a new "fast-food outlet" was opening near the campus, the class at once imagined rolls and chowmein. This is:
options: Anchoring: estimating from the first number seen
Representativeness: judging by fit with a prototype
Mental accounting: keeping separate budgets
The decoy: comparing with an inferior option
questions.why: The outlet might serve healthy food, but "fast food" fits a stereotype.

questions.q: After the outcry over New Coke, Coca-Cola:
options: Kept New Coke on sale and withdrew the original formula for good
Halved the price of New Coke until its sales recovered a year later
Brought the original back within about three months as Coca-Cola Classic
Renamed New Coke as Diet Coke and aimed it at a different segment
questions.why: The taste tests had never asked how people would feel about losing the original.

questions.q: In a preference-based segmentation chart, a bar to the right of the 0% line means that the segment:
options: Rates that variable as more important than the average customer does
Spends more on that variable than the average customer does
Is larger than the other segments, measured on that variable
Is less satisfied than the average customer on that variable
questions.why: The 0% line is the average of all respondents.

questions.q: On an MDS map, a brand sits on the "sporty" side. The correct reading is that it is:
options: The sportiest car on the market, since the axis measures sportiness
Sportier than the average of the brands rated, not necessarily a sports car
A sports car by definition, whatever its price or its features
Disliked by buyers who prefer chauffeur-driven, traditional cars
questions.why: Positions are relative; the centre is the average of all the brands rated.

questions.q: Under Mercedes-Benz India's "Retail of the Future" model, who sets the price, holds the stock and invoices the customer?
options: Each dealer, as before
An online marketplace
The customer's financier
Mercedes-Benz India itself
questions.why: Dealers became franchise partners who compete only on the customer's experience.

questions.q: The story of the cement company's 25-kg bags, whose seals broke when dealers threw them off trucks, was told to show that:
options: Small packs rarely sell in categories that are normally bought in bulk
Dealers should not be given a new product without training and incentives
Advertising and launch buzz are wasted if the product and its supply are not ready
Heavy marketing does not work for products that buyers see as commodities
questions.why: By the time the improved bags arrived, the buzz had died.

questions.q: "Customers want products that are available and affordable; make them efficiently and they will sell." This belief belongs to the:
options: Selling concept
Production concept
Marketing concept
Societal marketing concept
questions.why: The earliest of the four approaches: the grandfather's sweet shop, the only one in town.

questions.q: Low margins per unit in confectionery mean that a brand needs:
options: High volumes, and therefore strong distribution
A small, loyal group of buyers who pay more
Exclusive outlets in the largest cities only
A premium price to make up for low volumes
questions.why: A typical problem of low-involvement categories.

questions.q: In the psychologist's view of the buyer, behaviour is:
options: Rational, aimed at maximum benefit for minimum cost, and so predictable
Driven only by price and income, and so predictable from demographics
Subjective, shaped by upbringing and culture, and therefore unpredictable
Rational within limits, relying on shortcuts that give predictable errors
questions.why: It is the opposite extreme from the economist's rational, predictable buyer.

questions.q: The professor's tip for reading a case was that the main dilemma is usually stated in:
options: The exhibits at the back
The section on the company's history
The footnotes
The introduction, the conclusion, or both
questions.why: Case writers like to close the loop by repeating the issue at the end.

questions.q: "For [target market], [x] provides [point of difference], because [reason to believe]." Which element does this template leave out?
options: The target
The frame of reference
The point of difference
The reason to believe
questions.why: Templates mix and match the elements; some omit one.

questions.q: Lay's keeps adding flavours. One advantage of such line extensions noted in class is that they:
options: Let a bored customer switch without leaving the brand
Remove the need to invest in distribution for each flavour
Allow a higher price to be charged for every new flavour
Stop competitors from launching flavours of their own
questions.why: Otherwise the customer who wants a change moves to a rival snack.

questions.q: In the first case discussion, one proposal was to launch a premium line under the struggling brand's name. The professor's objection was that:
options: Brand extensions rarely work, so the company should always create a new brand instead
Premium products cannot be sold to customers who first met the brand as students
The proposal ignored the cost of the extra advertising that a premium line would need
An extension cannot be built on a weak parent; it should have been proposed while the brand was strong
questions.why: The same move is proactive from strength and desperate from weakness.

questions.q: How long does it take to build a strong brand that pulls customers without discounts?
options: About six months
Two to five years
Decades
One good advertising campaign
questions.why: The few that seem to rise in two or three years are survivors of thousands that failed.

questions.q: For services, the marketing mix is usually extended to seven Ps by adding:
options: People, Process and Physical evidence
Packaging, Positioning and People
Profit, Process and Partners
Purpose, People and Planet
questions.why: A service is produced and consumed in the same moment, by staff the customer can see.

questions.q: People say "Xerox" for a photocopy and ask for "Bisleri" when they want bottled water. Such names are called:
options: Fighter brands
Generic brands
Store brands
Ingredient brands
questions.why: The brand name has become the name of the category.

questions.q: The Taj group's Vivanta and Ginger were cited to show that:
options: A mass brand can move up easily if it changes its name
Hotel brands cannot be extended without losing their image
A premium brand can offer a cheaper line and be accepted
Repositioning a premium brand always damages the parent
questions.why: Moving down is easier than moving up.

questions.q: FMCG firms usually prefer to reduce the grams in a Rs. 10 pack rather than raise its price to Rs. 11 because:
options: Buyers notice a change in quantity more than a change in price
Retailers refuse to handle odd prices
Smaller packs are cheaper to transport
Demand can drop sharply when a price crosses a familiar threshold
questions.why: Buyers react more to price than to quantity, and Rs. 10 is a threshold.

questions.q: A pack offers "50% more" for the same price. The equivalent price cut is about:
questions.why: New price per unit = old price / 1.5, which is two-thirds of the old price.

questions.q: The sensitive-teeth segment is small in numbers, but its members brush twice a day without fail. This shows that:
options: Small segments should be ignored until they have grown large enough
Demographic variables always matter more than behavioural ones
The number of buyers is the only measure of a segment's worth
Usage can make a small segment more attractive than its size suggests
questions.why: Consumption depends on how many buy and how much each uses.

questions.q: A market leader rarely runs advertising that names a smaller rival because:
options: It hands the rival free publicity and a place beside the leader in the buyer's mind
Comparative advertising is something only a challenger is permitted to run
A leader has no need to advertise at all once it has reached the top
Customers nearly always side with the smaller brand in such comparisons
questions.why: Comparative advertising borrows the leader's fame, so it is the challenger's tool.

questions.q: The same company's cost of sales to prime customers was four to five times higher because:
options: Prime customers were smaller hospitals spread over a much wider geographic area
Prime customers bought the most expensive systems and demanded longer demonstrations
Its sales force kept pushing service and innovation those customers neither valued nor could afford
It had too few salespeople, so each call on a prime customer took far longer to arrange
questions.why: One selling approach for two different segments wastes money on one of them.

questions.q: In which stage of the product life cycle do sales flatten, competitors multiply and me-too offers appear?
options: Introduction
Maturity
Growth
Decline
questions.why: The objective there is to defend and differentiate.

questions.q: Saffola moved from advertisements about heart patients to everyday healthy cooking for families. Its reason for repositioning was to:
options: Correct a positioning that had gone wrong
Respond to a product recall
Reach a wider segment and expand its customer base
Move from a mass market to a niche
questions.why: It did so by changing its communication.

questions.q: Hierarchical clustering begins by:
options: Treating every respondent as a separate cluster and merging the closest, step by step
Fixing the number of clusters wanted and placing that many random starting points
Dividing the respondents by age and income before any ratings are compared
Removing the respondents whose ratings differ most from those of the majority
questions.why: K-means works the other way round: the analyst chooses k first.

questions.q: The central lesson of the Samsung story that opened the module is that:
options: A firm should keep cutting its price until customers notice the product
Advertising matters more than the product, the price or the channel
A challenger should avoid mentioning the market leader in its advertising
A good product still has to be made to mean something to the customer it is meant for
questions.why: The phones were good all along; what changed between 2011 and 2012 was what people knew and felt about them.

questions.q: In the professor's view, the biggest problem with Bic for Her was:
options: The "for her" labelling
The colour of the ink
The quality of the pen
The choice of retailers
questions.why: Placed quietly on the shelf, the pens might have found a small segment.

questions.q: The technical reason the professor gave for ChotuKool's limited success was that it:
options: Used so much electricity that the monthly bill ran into three digits
Could not hold a low temperature in states where summers cross 40 to 45 degrees
Was too heavy to be carried to a repair shop when it needed servicing
Had too many moving parts and needed servicing every few months
questions.why: Her deeper explanation, though, was researcher bias.

questions.q: The definition of segmentation speaks of "actual and/or potential customers". The word potential means that:
options: Only future customers, not present ones, should be studied
Segments must be of roughly equal size to be worth serving
People who do not buy today are left out of the exercise
You segment the whole possible market, not only today's buyers
questions.why: Non-users can be the most interesting segment of all.

questions.q: "Kitna deti hai?" summed up an industry assumption that Renault Kwid challenged. The assumption was that:
options: High-price car buyers care only about mileage and resale
Young buyers do not want a small car as their first car
Low-price car buyers care only about economy and mileage
Indian car buyers pay little attention to the price
questions.why: Kwid looked at the same buyers through psychographics and offered aspirational features.

questions.q: In the healthcare-equipment example, the primary decision makers in the key and the prime segments were, respectively:
options: Nurses and administrators
Administrators and nurses
Doctors and patients
Purchase managers and finance heads
questions.why: The two segments bought for different reasons and needed different selling.

questions.q: For a new breakfast cereal, which letter of PESTLE did the class give the most weight?
options: Technological, whether a 4G product will look dated in a 5G world
Political: how stable the government of a neighbouring country is
Legal: the emission and certification norms for electronic devices
Social: the move towards health-conscious and organic eating
questions.why: The framework stays the same; the emphasis moves with the product. For the smartphone it was technology.

questions.q: Which pair of methods captures what people do rather than what they say?
options: Surveys and polls
Eye tracking and A/B tests
In-depth interviews and focus groups
Concept tests and taste tests
questions.why: Both record actual behaviour, not stated preference.

questions.q: In business markets, "centralised or decentralised purchasing" and "purchase policies" belong to which base?
options: Firmographics
Benefits sought
Buying approach
Geographic
questions.why: It is the business-market cousin of psychographics.

questions.q: Documents disclosed in Apple's court battles over design were cited in class because they showed that:
options: Apple did a good deal of customer research, whatever it said in public
Apple had copied several of its rivals' designs before launching its own
Customers are unable to describe what they want in a new product
Research had led Apple into several product failures it later hid
questions.why: The lesson is to fix how research is done, not to abandon it.

questions.q: Maruti's difficulty with the Jimny was used in class to show that:
options: Off-road vehicles have no real market among car buyers in Indian cities
An established image of economy and value does not easily carry a lifestyle product
Maruti's dealers were unwilling to stock a car aimed at so small a segment
A good product will always overcome the image of the brand that sells it
questions.why: Repositioning is very risky territory, even with a good product.

questions.q: In the AMA's 2007 definition, the phrase "exchanging offerings that have value" brings in which P?
options: Product
Place
Promotion
Price
questions.why: Value is traded, not handed over. Creating is Product, communicating is Promotion, delivering is Place.

questions.q: In a positioning statement, the frame of reference is:
options: The proof that makes customers believe the brand's claim
The group of customers the brand has chosen to serve
The category or alternatives the brand is benchmarked against
The price band in which the brand has chosen to compete
questions.why: It tells customers what kind of thing the brand is.

questions.q: What does the societal marketing concept add to the marketing concept?
options: Heavier use of selling and promotion to move what the factory has already made
Satisfying customers in a way that also protects society's long-term interests
A focus on making products available and affordable through efficiency
Building the whole offering around what customers need and value
questions.why: The fourth approach, later written into the AMA's 2007 definition as "society at large".

questions.q: For a new toothpaste brand, the class thought a smaller, less crowded need could be a better place to start than a large one because:
options: A new player can get lost in a large, crowded segment
Large segments are nearly always unprofitable to serve
Small segments have no competitors in them at all
Retailers give more shelf space to niche products
questions.why: Size each need, then look at the competition in it.

questions.q: Why can "Linda is a bank teller and active in a feminist movement" never be more probable than "Linda is a bank teller"?
options: Bank tellers are rarely interested in social causes of any kind whatever
The description of Linda says nothing at all about the work that she does
The first is a subset of the second: two conditions must hold instead of one
Probability cannot be applied to judgements about individual people
questions.why: Fit with the description overrode the arithmetic.

questions.q: In the Nano's intended positioning, the differentiation was meant to be:
options: The lowest price of any car in the world
Sporty styling aimed at college students
Luxury features packed into a small car
Quality and robustness at that price: value
questions.why: "Cheapest car" was the media's position for it, not the company's.

questions.q: A participant called one-third of respondents willing to buy "a bad number". The professor's response was:
options: Any figure below 50% is a failure
Bad compared with what? A number needs a reference point
The figure should be doubled to allow for error
Research numbers should be ignored in a case
questions.why: Judge a number against a target, a competitor or a category norm.

questions.q: A customer gives a margin of Rs. 500 a year for 20 certain years. Discounted at 10%, these are worth about Rs. 4,257, and the customer cost Rs. 1,500 to acquire. The CLV is about:
questions.why: Net present value: 4,257 less the acquisition cost of 1,500.

questions.q: Driving is statistically riskier than flying, yet flying feels riskier just after a crash. The reason given in class is that:
options: People anchor on the price of the ticket when judging the risk
Airlines frame their safety record as a loss instead of a gain
Flying is booked into a separate mental account from driving
Vivid, recent events are easily recalled and so feel more likely
questions.why: Availability: what comes to mind easily is judged more probable.

questions.q: In the keep-or-drop decision on a brand, contribution means:
options: The brand's share of total sales
Profit after allocated fixed costs
Price minus variable cost
Revenue minus advertising
questions.why: Fixed costs remain whether or not the brand exists, so they should not drive the decision.

questions.q: The slide "Marketing Management: The Plan" names three activities: situation analysis, developing strategy and designing tactics. In that order, they are:
options: The 5Cs, STP and the 4Ps
STP, the 5Cs and the 4Ps
The 4Ps, STP and the 5Cs
PESTLE, the 4Ps and STP
questions.why: Read the situation, choose the strategy, then carry it out.
